Let's step into Chapter 2: How Human Progress Has Changed the Planet.
Picture this—back in the early days of television, families used to gather around tiny screens, watching black-and-white images of wild animals and distant lands. For most, it was their very first look at the wider world—a place that felt almost infinite, completely out of reach. I mean, who could imagine that humans would ever leave a lasting mark on a planet so vast?
But as time rolled forward, that idea started to change. The signs became harder to overlook. People were everywhere. Cities kept growing, and the demand for food, fresh water, and energy shot up. If you looked down from space, satellites revealed forests turning into patchwork fields, rivers being dammed or rerouted, and coastlines reshaped to make room for development.
Imagine being a young scientist, eager to make sense of all these changes. You might start with the numbers. Back in the 1950s, Earth was home to about two and a half billion people. Fast forward to the year 2000, and that number had doubled—more than six billion. Every single person needed food, shelter, and power. So, forests got cleared, wetlands were drained, and wild places were transformed to meet those needs.
The speed of this transformation is honestly mind-blowing. In just a few decades, more than half of the world’s rainforests vanished. Grasslands that had stretched for miles were plowed under to grow crops. Oceans that once teemed with fish started to empty out, thanks to massive industrial fleets. Those endless wild places? Suddenly, they were hemmed in by roads, towns, and farms.
Yet, most people never saw these changes up close. Food showed up in supermarkets. Water flowed from the tap. Electricity kept the lights on. That direct link to nature—the one our grandparents knew—started to fade. It was easy to believe that nature was still out there, untouched and unchanged.
But, if you looked a little closer, the warning signs were everywhere. Coral reefs—sometimes called the rainforests of the sea—were bleaching and dying as oceans warmed. Insects, those tiny workers that pollinate crops and recycle nutrients, began to disappear. Birds and mammals vanished at rates not seen since the days of the dinosaurs.
Here’s the thing: human prosperity is deeply connected to the planet’s health. The air we breathe, the water we drink, the food on our plates—all of it depends on the natural world. Cut down forests, and the climate changes. Exhaust the soil, and crops fail. Collapse the fish stocks, and entire communities feel the pain.
Some people tried to raise the alarm, but their voices were often drowned out by the rush of daily life. Progress was mostly measured in dollars and growth, not in the health of forests or the abundance of wildlife. The loss of nature was brushed off—as if it were simply the price of progress, a necessary trade-off for a better life.
But here’s something we shouldn’t overlook: beneath all that growth, the hidden costs were piling up. The world was becoming less stable, less resilient. The systems that had supported life on Earth for millions of years were being pushed right to the edge.
So now, the real question isn’t whether people can change the planet. We know we can. The question is—can the planet keep supporting us?
